name: Teal
lede: Teal is a dark greenish blue named after the colored band on the wing of a small duck, and on screens it is the web color #008080.

sections.title: A duck's wing
sections.body:
Teal is the name of a small freshwater duck, and the color takes its name from the dark greenish-blue band on the bird's wing [1][2]. Paterson's dictionary defines it that way and adds that it is also called teal blue [1]. St Clair's list of color-name origins gives much the same gloss: a strong green with a dash of blue [2].

As a color word it is young. Our word-history data records 1917 as the earliest use of teal as a color name in English [3]. The duck, though, was already in the color charts a century before that, as an example rather than a name, as the next section shows [4].

sections.title: The bird in the old charts
sections.body:
In 1821 Patrick Syme's edition of Werner's *Nomenclature of Colours* used the teal drake to illustrate three different colors, none of them teal [4][5][6]. The beauty spot on its wing stands for emerald green, number 53 in the chart [4]. Syme's gloss on that color is that it is about equal parts Berlin blue and gamboge yellow, so the wing patch he had in mind was a green, not the blue-green we now call teal [4]. See [[emerald-green]] for the pigment-minded reading.

The drake's breast illustrates cream yellow, which Syme took over from Werner's Isabella yellow [5]. Its neck illustrates deep reddish brown, number 101 [6]. The duck was evidently a handy source of colors, but what it illustrated was a green and two warm tones, and the word *teal* did not yet name a color.

Pastoureau offers a different, modern use of the word. Heraldic azure is a bare word in a blazon, and artists rendered it as a bright blue, sometimes as a teal and sometimes as a dark shade, without changing the arms' meaning [8]. That is the writer's word, not a medieval one.

sections.title: The web color
sections.body:
On the web, Teal is one of the 140 colors of the X11 set, with hex code #008080 [7]. It is also among the 16 colors of the old VGA palette, next to aqua, navy, olive and purple [7]. In RGB it is 0, 128, 128, exactly half the strength of [[aqua]], which is 0, 255, 255 [3].

The swatch is a measured color, not a bird: lightness 48, chroma 30, hue 196 in LCH, which our matching places in the strong bluish green region of the 1955 ISCC-NBS system [3]. Its contrast ratio is 4.77 against white and 4.4 against black [3]. Other teals disagree with it. The xkcd color survey of 2010 produced a greener teal, #029386, about 8 units away from the web color [3]. Nearby names include [[teal-blue]], [[dark-cyan]], [[turquoise]] and [[dark-teal]] [3].

Paterson also records a ketchup sold in three mystery colors, pink, orange or teal, revealed only when the packaging came off; he gives no date [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Teal is rare in the paintings of our archive. It appears in 11 of 23,781 paintings, 0.05 per cent, and is rarer than 86 per cent of the named colors [9]. The earliest dated match is [[painting:rijks-200108437|a painting of 1520]], and the latest is [[painting:aic-9021|a canvas of 1913]]; only 7 dated paintings have it over at least 2 per cent of the canvas [9]. That 1520 match is 397 years before the earliest record of the word in our sources, so it is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not evidence of a pigment or dye [9]. All of these numbers are as photographed: museum images of varnished, yellowed paintings.

In printed English the adjective peaks in the 2010s and rose fastest in the 1990s, by Google Books counts of adjective use only [3].
